 Lu Dort knows his first return to Oklahoma City will be emotional and 'surreal'
 Now with the Hawks, Lu Dort and Aaron Wiggins are ready to face the Thunder -- the team they helped become perennial contenders.
 Shaun Powell
 Archive November 18, 2026 1:27 PM Lu Dort is averaging 8.9 points and 3.1 rebounds with the Hawks this season.
 There will be theater Wednesday when the Hawks visit Oklahoma City to create a pair of curious scenarios ( 8 ET, League Pass ).
 As the Thunder currently cope with a war of attrition caused suddenly by crucial injuries, they’ll face two former players who helped juice Oklahoma City’s great run of the last few years — Lu Dort and Aaron Wiggins — both traded to Atlanta last summer.
 Dort is one of the best defensive players this decade, and in this game, for the first time, he’ll be assigned to guard none other than Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, a matchup worth watching for different reasons.
 Every so often during the NBA season, there are showcase games, and this is one of them, for a November night, anyway. Nothing special is on the line, except pride and emotion and a strange coincidence.
 “Surreal,” said Dort. “That’s a good word.”
 The Thunder shipped Dort to the Hawks mainly to escape the luxury tax second apron, and because his replacement, Cason Wallace, was ready to assume the starting backcourt spot next to Shai.
 This decision didn’t catch Dort by surprise. Oklahoma City had been careening toward this crossroad by virtue of its exemplary track record for talent-stocking. The Thunder’s bench was perhaps on par with the starting lineups of other teams. Yet in the age of salary-cap restrictions, you can’t pay everyone.
 Team president Sam Presti, who created this good problem, maintained a consistent line of communication with Dort throughout last season regarding his future with OKC.
 “I knew something was going to happen,” Dort said. “I didn’t know where I would go. But it was done the right way.”
 Parting with Dort was awkward, anyway. He and Shai made for a well-balanced tandem. Shai developed as a masterful scorer, Dort as an aggressive lock-down defender who could also knock down a 3-pointer when opposing defenders doubled Shai. During this time, OKC flourished, winning the 2025 championship and averaging 62 wins while claiming the No. 1 seed over the last three seasons.
 Dort has a soft spot for OKC, the only city and team he knew until now, and vice versa. He was an undrafted free agent in 2019 and endeared himself to teammates and fans with his blue-collar approach to the game and island-cool demeanor; he’s from Montreal but his family roots are in Haiti. His NBA meal ticket was his toughness, which he leveraged on defense, quickly gaining a deserved reputation for challenging the other team’s most dangerous scorer.
 Dort helped raise the defensive awareness of the Thunder, one reason for the club’s recent success. He’ll surely receive a gushing welcome on Wednesday when OKC pays tribute.
 “A part of me will be there for life,” he said. “What we accomplished for the city and the state was amazing. Obviously going back and seeing some familiar faces will be good, seeing people from the organization, the staff and just being back to the city. I haven’t been back since I was traded. I’m grateful for my time there. And that banner will be up there for life.”
 Then the game will begin.
 And then a former All-Defensive first team member will deal with the ultimate test, and a weird one as well.
 Dort has guarded big players, quick players, long-distance shooters, rim attackers, etc. Now he gets assigned to a scoring genius. Dort has obvious respect for Shai. When asked the other day about the prospect of guarding him, Dort laughed playfully and said, “I’ll try to be the one to stop him.”
 Then he pointed in the direction of Wiggins, who stood nearby.
 “Me and him,” Dort said, with more laughter as Wiggins shot a surprised expression. “Yeah, I’m going to put your name in there, too.”
 Dort does bring experience, having practiced against Shai many times in their seven years together, and that’s not including their time on the Canadian national team. Yet he’s quick to say: “Obviously it’ll be different.”
 Specifically, Shai’s ability to draw fouls by baiting physical defenders into making contact will be especially interesting against Dort. Does Dort fall for those tactics and send Shai to the free-throw line?
 “He thinks about that all the time, how to get that advantage,” said Dort. “What he’s using is skills and IQ to put defenders in a bad position, to foul him. So I don’t think this is going to change. Playing against a player like that, you’ve got to be aware of the physicality that you use. I’ll play him the same way, though.”
 Shai is the David Blaine of basketball, however, bringing more tricks and deception than most. He doesn’t just beat a path to the free throw line. He has a trademark mid-range game, ability to attack the rim and will on occasion shoot 3-pointers. Over the last four seasons he averaged at least 30 points and is on pace to make it five straight, currently at 30.9, with 30 points in four of his last five games.
 “I know how he moves,” Dort said. “Actually, nothing really fazes him. He’s really confident, and whenever he gets to his spots he’s really comfortable, so I’ve seen him do well against a lot of tough defenders. It’s just the type of player he is.”
 Dort said the best option is to throw and rotate not just multiple defenders at Shai, but good defenders with different body types and tendencies. In the case of the Hawks, they’re equipped to do just that.
 Dort isn’t the only All-Defensive team member; there’s Dyson Daniels, a ball hawk who’s taller and strips even the best dribblers. Nickeil Alexander-Walker, who happens to be Shai’s cousin, brings very solid perimeter defense, along with Wiggins, who, like Dort, had his share of practice reps against Shai.
 “It’s a team thing,” said Dort. “We’ve got to do it as a team to stop a guy like that. He’s a great player, really good scorer and he has so many ways to score, so it takes a team to stop a guy like that.”
 Shai is under siege somewhat at the moment, a trapeze artist working without a net. His trademark shooting efficiency has dipped; Shai is at 47% after four straight seasons at 51% or higher.
 There’s a reason: Defenses are locked on him, more than usual, because of the circumstances. Jalen Williams is likely done for the season after surgery for a fractured left fibula and dislocated ankle. Chet Holmgren might be out until midseason following a patellar tendon tear.
 And Dort’s replacement might also miss the season; Wallace had surgery to repair a torn labrum. Williams, Holmgren and Wallace have played just three games and combined to average over 32 points.
 This makes for a peculiar situation for OKC, a team that could use Dort and Wiggins and also Isaiah Joe, now in Detroit, three rotational players traded away this offseason.
 In his role with the Hawks, Dort is coming off the bench regularly for the first time in his career. But he’s on the floor when it counts, especially when the Hawks need a smart defender against a top scorer.
 Which means, Dort should get more than a few reps Wednesday.
 “It’s gonna be good,” Dort said. “I’m looking forward to it. Obviously it’ll be something I’m not used to. I don’t know how I’ll feel. I’ll probably be a little shocked by the situation and I’ll have to lock back into the game, but that will be a surreal moment.”
 * * *
